c.tagline: Monuments, mass games and a capital frozen in revolutionary time.

taxi.fareNote: Foreign visitors almost always travel by tour van/bus with a guide rather than hailing taxis independently; metered cabs exist for hotel use and locals, payable in cash USD/EUR/RMB.

emergency.police: 110 (official but rarely functional/used by the public; report any incident immediately to your state-appointed tour guide)
emergency.medical: 8119 (official ambulance line); foreign visitors are typically taken to the Pyongyang Friendship Hospital for foreigners, coordinated by your tour guide
emergency.note: Independent action by foreign tourists is not permitted - always go through your guide first, who will liaise with authorities, your embassy, or an evacuation insurer if needed.

avoid.reason: Independent movement is prohibited — visitors may only go where their state-assigned guides take them, so off-itinerary areas are effectively all off-limits.
Never photograph military sites, checkpoints or leaders' images disrespectfully, never fold or discard images of the leaders, and never leave your group — violations carry severe consequences.

hood_desc: The monumental heart of the capital around Kim Il Sung Square, the Grand People's Study House and the Taedong riverfront; almost every organized tour itinerary is anchored here for easy access to the main state monuments.

A self-contained island compound in the Taedong River dominated by the 47-storey Yanggakdo International Hotel, effectively a walled resort with its own casino, bowling alley and revolving restaurant; suits tour groups who spend evenings on-site since leaving the island unaccompanied isn't permitted.
A green, spread-out district around Kim Il Sung's birthplace and the Sports Village/Kwangbok Street towers, commonly used for budget group tours, student and sports delegations.
A wooded park district built around Moran Hill with cherry blossoms in spring and views over the old city walls; a quieter, lower-key base used by smaller tour groups.
The riverside quarter along the Potong River near the old Potong Gate, mixing 1980s business-hotel blocks with department stores; a convenient economy option close to the city center.

water.note: Tourists are provided bottled water; avoid drinking tap water.

transit.pay: Foreign tourists generally do not use public transit independently; when a metro or tram ride is included in an itinerary, guides handle tickets/fares. Locals pay small won fares via paper tickets or transit cards on the metro and coins on trams/buses.
transit.hours: Roughly 5:30/6:00am to 9:30/10:00pm; there is no late-night or 24-hour service.
transit.note: Tourists typically ride only 1-2 designated, ornately decorated Pyongyang Metro stations (e.g., Puhung, Yonggwang) as part of a guided tour; unaccompanied use of public transit by foreigners is not permitted.

bus: Domestic long-distance coaches to Kaesong, Nampo, Wonsan and other provincial cities

transit.m: Train (Sunan Station on the Pyongui Line) to Pyongyang Station, ~20-25 min
Tour operator van/bus transfer (arranged as part of guided tour package)

tip.r: Tipping is not traditionally practiced in North Korea, but small tips for tour guides and drivers are increasingly accepted and appreciated at trip's end; not expected in restaurants.

food.name: Pyongyang Naengmyeon
food.desc: Chewy buckwheat noodles in chilled beef-and-radish broth with pear, cucumber and egg. The city's defining dish, eaten with scissors and vinegar.

places.name: Okryu-gwan
places.note: State-run since 1960 beside the Taedong; seats up to 2,000 and is the benchmark for the dish.

places.name: Chongryugwan
places.note: The other well-known cold-noodle house, a standard stop on organised itineraries.

places.name: Koryo Hotel restaurants
places.note: Hotel dining rooms where groups are often housed; naengmyeon is on the standard menu.

food.name: Sinsollo (Royal Hot Pot)
food.desc: A brass ring-shaped pot of clear broth arranged with meat, fish, egg ribbons, nuts and vegetables, simmered at the table. A Korean court dish.

places.name: Chongryu Hotpot Restaurant
places.note: Best known specifically for sinsollo and other hot pots; a frequent set-menu stop for visitors.

places.name: Okryu-gwan
places.note: Serves court-style dishes alongside its noodles when booked as part of a group meal.

places.name: Yanggakdo International Hotel restaurants
places.note: Large tourist hotel with several restaurants where hot pot appears on banquet menus.

food.name: Pyongyang Onban
food.desc: Rice topped with shredded chicken, mushrooms and a mung-bean pancake, then flooded with hot chicken broth. A local winter comfort dish.

places.name: Okryu-gwan
places.note: Serves the classic Pyongyang repertoire beyond noodles, onban included.

places.name: Chongryugwan
places.note: Traditional Pyongyang menu with onban and pancakes alongside the cold noodles.

places.name: Koryo Hotel restaurants
places.note: Reliable place to find regional dishes when a set itinerary allows a choice.

food.name: Nokdujijim
food.desc: Thick pancakes of ground mung bean fried crisp with pork, kimchi and scallion. Traditionally eaten with cold noodles or as a drinking snack.

places.name: Okryu-gwan
places.note: The classic pairing here is a mung-bean pancake ordered alongside the naengmyeon.

places.name: Taedonggang Beer Bar No. 3
places.note: State beer hall where fried snacks and pancakes are served with the draught.

places.name: Kwangbok Department Store food hall
places.note: Large public food hall where everyday Korean snacks are cooked to order.

food.name: Pyongyang Duck Barbecue
food.desc: Thin slices of duck grilled at the table over a domed hotplate, wrapped in lettuce with garlic, chilli paste and rice. A popular sit-down group meal.

places.name: Rakwon Duck Barbecue Restaurant
places.note: Long-established table-grill restaurant regularly included on organised tour itineraries.

places.name: Chongryu Hotpot Restaurant
places.note: Table cooking of meats as well as hot pots; a comparable communal grill experience.

places.name: Yanggakdo International Hotel restaurants
places.note: Barbecue and Korean grill options within the main tourist hotel complex.

food.name: Pyongyang Kimchi
food.desc: The northern style is milder and wetter than the southern: less chilli, more brine, often with pear and seafood. Buried in jars for winter.

places.name: Okryu-gwan
places.note: Kimchi is served with every meal; the mild northern style is the one to notice here.

places.name: Kwangbok Department Store food hall
places.note: Food hall and grocery floor selling kimchi and pickles as everyday household items.

places.name: Koryo Hotel restaurants
places.note: Banchan spreads with several kimchi types accompany hotel meals.

food.name: Taedonggang Beer
food.desc: State-brewed lager made on plant bought from a British brewery in 2000. Sold in numbered styles from pale to dark and served fresh at city beer halls.

places.name: Taedonggang Beer Bar No. 3
places.note: Public beer hall pouring the brewery's numbered styles; visits are arranged through tour operators.

places.name: Yanggakdo International Hotel bars
places.note: Hotel bars stock the full range; the simplest place for visitors to compare the styles.

places.name: Koryo Hotel bars
places.note: Central hotel bars serving draught and bottled Taedonggang in the evenings.

food.name: Insam (Ginseng) Tea
food.desc: Korean ginseng, one of the country's best-known exports, brewed into a bittersweet tea and often sweetened with honey. Served after meals.

places.name: Koryo Hotel restaurants
places.note: Ginseng tea and ginseng products are a standard part of hotel service and shops.

places.name: Okryu-gwan
places.note: Traditional teas are poured after the noodle courses at group meals.

places.name: Kwangbok Department Store
places.note: Sells packaged ginseng tea and honey alongside its food hall; a common souvenir stop.

landmarks: Juche Tower
A 170-meter granite spire topped with a red illuminated flame, honoring North Korea's Juche ideology and offering the city's best panoramic viewpoint.
Kim Il Sung Square
The vast central plaza famous for its massive military parades and mass rallies, flanked by monumental government buildings along the Taedong River.
Arch of Triumph
Modeled on and taller than the Parisian original, this granite arch commemorates Korean resistance to Japanese occupation and Kim Il Sung's return in 1945.
Mansudae Grand Monument
Two towering bronze statues of North Korea's former leaders dominate Mansu Hill, the country's most solemn and heavily visited monument.
Ryugyong Hotel
An enormous 105-story pyramid-shaped skyscraper that dominates the Pyongyang skyline, instantly recognizable as the city's most futuristic silhouette.
Pyongyang Metro
Among the world's deepest subway systems, its ornate stations feature marble columns, chandeliers, and vivid mosaics evoking Soviet-era grandeur.
Grand People's Study House
A sweeping traditional-roofed library overlooking Kim Il Sung Square, symbolizing the state's emphasis on mass education and study.
Monument to Party Founding
Three massive stone fists gripping hammer, sickle, and writing brush celebrate the Workers' Party's founding ideals of worker, farmer, and intellectual unity.
Mangyongdae Native House
The humble thatched-roof birthplace of Kim Il Sung, preserved as a pilgrimage site illustrating the founding leader's officially told origin story.
Moranbong Park
A scenic hilltop park of ancient pavilions, fortress ruins, and gardens above the Taedong River, popular for cherry blossoms and city views.

intl.op: Korean State Railway / China Railway (booked via authorised tour operators)

dom.op: Korean State Railway — travel only on a pre-arranged organised tour, no public booking

train.note: The twice-weekly Pyongyang-Dandong-Beijing sleeper (K27/K28) resumed in early 2026 after a six-year pandemic halt, but you cannot just buy a ticket: foreigners may only enter North Korea on a pre-arranged organised tour (e.g. via Koryo Tours or Young Pioneer Tours), and US passport holders remain barred. The long-planned Moscow/Russia through trains had not reliably resumed as of mid-2026. Treat all of this as subject to sudden change.

bus.note: There is no public international bus service. All foreign travel in and out of North Korea is tightly controlled and arranged through a licensed tour company; independent overland coach travel is not possible.

ferry.note: No scheduled passenger ferry operates from Pyongyang (its port is Nampho). A Russia-DPRK sea link has historically run from Rajin/Rason to Vladivostok rather than from the capital, and its passenger service has been intermittent - do not count on it.

half.name: Sariwŏn
half.blurb: North Korean provincial city known as a regional agricultural and industrial center.

full.name: Seoul

full.blurb: Major port city with a lively Chinatown, waterfront parks, and international airport.
